```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library (tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
```

### Problem 1

**Step 1: import and clean data**
```{r import}
data("ny_noaa") #load dataset into environment

noaa_df <- ny_noaa #assign into df, no need to convert missing values to NA since it's 'pre-built' into file

noaa_df = janitor::clean_names(noaa_df)

print(noaa_df, n = 5) #shows that column names converted correctly and that first 16 rows contains no data

```
**Preliminary Data description:**
This dataset contains `r ncol(noaa_df)` variables named: "id", "date", "prcp", "snow", "snwd", "tmax" and "tmin". In these 7 columns, it contains `r nrow(noaa_df)` observations with its weather station ID ("id"), date of observation ("date"), precipitation to tenths of mm ("prcp"), snowfall to mm ("snow"), snow depth to mm ("snwd"), and min max temperature to tenths of Celsius ("tmin", "tmax"). The extent to which missing data is an issue depends on what questions you want to answer as well as if the data missing can be inferred from other data in the same row. For example if you want to ask about precipitation levels for a certain time period in which the column 'prcp' is empty, then that would be a major issue. However, variables like 'snwd' could probably be inferred from 'snow'. Especially with `r nrow(noaa_df)` amount of entries even if you can't directly calculate 'snwd' given 'snow', you can just look at other entries with the same 'snow' value and copy it in. These are just two examples to show that missing data can be a very big issue or a relatively smaller one depending on your question and specific circumstances. 

**Step 2: Data Manipulation**
```{r noaa_manipulation}
noaa_df <- ny_noaa %>% #This creates separate variables for year, month and day and converts observations of temperature, precipitation and snowfall into more convenient scales (from mm or tenths of mm to cm and from tenths of degrees celsius to degrees celsius) 
  mutate(year = year(date),
         month = month(date),
         day = day(date),
         tmax_1deg = as.numeric(tmax)/10, #1C = 10 tenths of degrees celsius
         tmin_1deg = as.numeric(tmin)/10, #1C = 10 tenths of degrees celsius
         prcp_cm = prcp/100, #1 cm = 100 tenths of mm
         snow_cm = snow/10, #1 cm = 10 mm
         snwd_cm = snwd/10) #1 cm = 10 mm

print(n = 5, noaa_df, width = Inf)#Checked to see that new columns (variables) made correctly. 

mc_snow <- noaa_df %>%
  count(snow_cm) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1) 

mc_snwd <- noaa_df %>%
  count(snwd_cm) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1)# shows results in tibble, most common value for both is '0' and shows up 1597641 times. 

mc_snowil <- mc_snow %>%
  pull(snow_cm)

mc_snwdil <- mc_snwd %>%
  pull(snwd_cm)
```
**Comment:**
For snowfall, the most common values for "snow_cm" and "snwd_cm" are `r mc_snowil` and `r mc_snwdil` respectively. This is because in New York where the weather data is being collected, most days out of the year don't snow. 

**Step 3: Data Visualization**
```{r noaa_visualization}
#January plot: 
jan_noaa <- noaa_df %>%
  filter(month == 1) %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax_1deg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in Janurary 1981-2010",
    x ="", 
    y = "Avg max Temp (°C)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
#July plot: 
july_noaa <- noaa_df %>%
filter(month == 7) %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax_1deg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, color = "tomato") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in July 1981-2010",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Avg max Temp (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Combine using patchwork operators
jan_noaa / july_noaa
```
There doesn't seem to be any trend with temperatures within the same ranges (about -5 to 10C for Jan and 20-30C for July) across the period observed (1981-2010). However, the stations generally trend up and down 'together' and so we see bold thick lines going up and down together. However, outliers do exist trending at times opposite to the majority instead of just trending 'too much' in the direction of the majority. Examples include the two large downward spikes between 1980-1990 in the "July" plot and a few peaks upwards between 2000-2005 in the "January" plot. 

**Step 3 cont: Data Visualization**
```{r p2}
p1 <- noaa_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin_1deg, y = tmax_1deg)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis")
  labs(
    title = "Panel (i): Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Min Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Max Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- noaa_df %>%
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue", color = "darkblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(
    title = "Panel (ii): Snowfall Distribution by Year (0 < Snowfall < 100)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

# Combine vertically using patchwork
p1 / p2
```

### Problem 2

**Step 1: Load, tidy and merge**
```{r import2}
acc_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_accel.csv",
                   na = c("", "NA", "."))|>
          janitor::clean_names()

demo_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
                    skip = 4,
                    na = c("", "NA", "."))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |>
          drop_na() |>
          filter(age >= 21)
          
print(acc_df)
print(demo_df) #this is to check that the skip = 4, na conversions, drop_na, age < 21 dropped, clean_names all worked

demo_df <- demo_df %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert sex: 1 = male, 2 = female
    sex = factor(sex, 
                 levels = c(1, 2), 
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    # Convert education: 1 = less than highschool, 2 = highschool equivalent, 3 = more than highschool
    education = factor(education, 
                       levels = c(1, 2, 3), 
                       labels = c("Less than high school", 
                                  "High school equivalent", 
                                  "More than high school"))
  )

merged_df <- demo_df %>%
  full_join(acc_df, by = "seqn")

print(n = 25, merged_df) #shows properly merged, clean and tidy df ready for manipulation
```
**Step 2: Table Creation**
```{r table}
edu_by_sex <- merged_df %>%
  drop_na(sex, education) %>%
  count(education, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

print(edu_by_sex) #Checks that table works

knitr::kable(
  edu_by_sex,
  col.names = c("Education Category", "Male", "Female"),
  caption = "Table 1. Number of Men and Women Across Education Categories"
)

male1 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'Less than high school') %>%
  pull(Male)

male2 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'High school equivalent') %>%
  pull(Male)

male3 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'More than high school') %>%
  pull(Male)

female1 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'Less than high school') %>%
  pull(Female)

female2 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'High school equivalent') %>%
  pull(Female)

female3  <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'More than high school') %>%
  pull(Female)

```
**Comment on Male and Female by Education Cat Table:**
From the table, we see that males and females with less than high school education are `r male1` and `r female1` respectively. males and females with high school equivalent education are `r male2` and `r female2` respectively and finally, males and females with higher than highs school education are `r male3` and `r female3` respectively. The dataset is mostly balanced between Male and Female with the greatest difference being `r male2-female2` between Male and Female who received high school equivalent education. 

**Step 3: Visualization**
```{r agedist_visualization}
#Create the visualization for age distributions
age_dist_plot <- merged_df %>%
  drop_na(age, sex, education) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Education Category and Sex",
    x = "Education Category",
    y = "Age (Years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1), 
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")

# Print the plot
print(age_dist_plot)
```
**Comment on age distribution by education cat and sex plot:**
The mean ages for each education category between the 2 sexes are quite similar. With the 'Less than high school' category having a mean female age of `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` and a mean male age of `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. Then in the 'High school equivalent' category, the mean female age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` while the mean male age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. Finally in the 'More than Highschool' category, the mean female age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` while the mean male age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. The range of ages goes from about 30 upwards to about 75 across education categories and sex. There is also a downwards trend in mean age observable in both sexes from the 'less than highschool' category until the youngest category of 'more than highschool'.

**Step 3 cont.: Visualization**
```{r activityviz}
#Visualization of total activity over the day

# Aggregate across minute columns to create a total activity variable for each participant
# starts_with("min") targets all minute-by-minute activity columns automatically
activity_summary <- merged_df %>%
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(select(., starts_with("min")), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Create the plot comparing men to women, with age on the x-axis, 
# total activity on the y-axis, and faceted by education level
activity_summary %>%
  drop_na(age, total_activity, sex, education) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex, fill = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.3) + # Scatter points with slight transparency
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) + # Smooth trend lines with confidence intervals
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 1) + # Separate panels stacked vertically for each education category
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity vs. Age by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```
***Total Daily Activity Comment***
All three graphs generally follow a slight downwards trend as age increases but stay mostly stable. In the "less than highschool' category, men generally had higher levels of Total Daily Activity when the opposite is true for the other two plots for the other education categories. 

```{r 24h}
# Visualization of activity of day but 24-hour time course

# Pivot minute-level accelerometer columns to long format while keeping demographic variables
time_course_long <- merged_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"), 
    names_to = "minute_col", 
    values_to = "activity"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract the numeric minute value from column names like "min1" -> 1
    minute = readr::parse_number(minute_col)
  )

# Calculate the mean activity for each combination of education, sex, and minute
plot_data <- time_course_long %>%
  drop_na(education, sex, minute, activity) %>%
  group_by(education, sex, minute) %>%
  summarize(mean_activity = mean(activity, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Create the three-panel time-course plot using minute on the x-axis
plot_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_activity, color = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 1) + # Creates three stacked panels for each education tier[cite: 3]
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Time Courses by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Minute of the Day (1 to 1440)",
    y = "Mean Activity Level (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1440, by = 240)) # Adds tick marks every 4 hours (240 minutes)
```

***Comments on 24-Hour activity plot:***
From the general trend, we can see the low mean activity level from minutes 0-360 when people are generally asleep across sex and education level. Then activity makes a sharp rise until about 480 which corresponds to 8AM when people get up to start their daily activities. Finally we see across all three educational levels that there is a daytime plateau which starts to trend downwards at around 1200 minutes which is about 10pm when people begin to go to bed. 

In terms of sex differences, in the "more than highschool" plot we see that females average slightly higher activity level throughout the day compared to the other two in which the male and female lines basically overlap. This suggests subtle differences in daytime activity distribution or volume among higher-educated cohorts.

### Problem 3

***Step 1: Data import, clean and tidy***
```{r importciti}
# Import and clean 
jan_2020_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
                        na = c("", "NA", ".")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "January")

july_2020_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/July 2020 Citi.csv",
                         na = c("", "NA", ".")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "July")

jan_2024_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
                        na = c("", "NA", ".")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "January")

july_2024_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/July 2024 Citi.csv",
                         na = c("", "NA", ".")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "July")

# Check the imports
print(jan_2020_df)
print(july_2020_df)
print(jan_2024_df)
print(july_2024_df)

# Join them all into one master dataset 
citibike_combined_df <- bind_rows(
  jan_2020_df,
  july_2020_df,
  jan_2024_df,
  july_2024_df
)

# Check the final combined dataset
glimpse(citibike_combined_df[13000, ]) #Merged dataset clean and tidy, also nothing wrong with mutating in month and year
```
***Data Description***
The resulting dataset contains `r `ncol(citibike_combined_df)` columns with the variables: ride_id, rideable_type, weekdays, duration, start_station, end_station, member_casual, month and year. There are `r nrow(citibike_combined_df)` total rows in the dataset with each row representing a ride. The year and month columns were added in for later use down the line and all rows and columns (which are same across 4 files) kept in 'merge'. 

***Step 2: Make Table 1***
```{r tableciti}
# Aggregate and pivot the data to show rides by year, month, and rider type
rides_by_time_user <- citibike_combined_df %>%
  drop_na(year, month, member_casual) %>%
  count(year, month, member_casual) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual, 
    values_from = n, 
    values_fill = 0
  )

# Check the tibble structure in the console
print(rides_by_time_user)

# Create a reader-friendly formatted table using knitr::kable
knitr::kable(
  rides_by_time_user,
  col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member"),
  caption = "Table 1. Total Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Rider Type"
)
```
***Table 1 comments:***
In the table, July 2024 had the highest number of causal riders as well as member rides (`r rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July") %>% pull(casual)` and `r rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July") %>% pull(member)`, respectively). The member rides keeps increasing over time with the largest increase happening between 2024 Jan and July (`r (rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July") %>% pull(member))- (rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "January") %>% pull(member))` increase in rides). The causal rides generally increase as well, however, there is a dip from July 2020 to January 2024 (`r rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2020, month == "July") %>% pull(casual)` to `r rides_by_time_user %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "January") %>% pull(casual)`). 

***Step 2: Make Table 2***
```{r table2}
# Calculate the top 5 starting stations for July 2024
top_start_stations_24 <- citibike_combined_df %>%
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") %>%
  drop_na(start_station_name) %>%
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

#  Check the table in the console
print(top_start_stations_24)

# Create a table using knitr::kable
knitr::kable(
  top_start_stations_24,
  col.names = c("Starting Station Name", "Number of Rides"),
  caption = "Table 2. Top 5 Most Popular Starting Stations for July 2024"
)
```

***Step 3: Data Visualization 1***
```{r durationplot}
#Calculate median ride duration across year, month, and day of the week
median_duration_df <- citibike_combined_df %>%
  drop_na(year, month, weekdays, duration) %>%
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) %>%
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Optional: Reorder days of the week chronologically (Monday - Sunday)
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  )

# Check the summarized table
print(median_duration_df)

# Create the comparison plot
median_duration_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, fill = month)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) + # Side-by-side bars comparing months within days
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 2) +             # Separate panels for each year (2020 vs 2024)
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of the Week, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)", #Duration assumed to be in minutes according to google search
    fill = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")
```
***Plot 1 observations:***
We see that across both plots, median ride duration, that point at which 50% of ride duration is lower or higher, is longer during July compared to January. This makes sense because people tend to be outside more and ride bikes more during the summer months when the weather is nice. But while the median duration for January hasn't changed much across the two years, median duration for July 2020 were much longer than duration for July 2024. This is probably because bike riding was a socially distanced activity you could do outside during the pandemic. But in general, people rode the citibikes at longer median durations in 2020. Over the weekdays the median duration is relatively stable but rising for the weekends. This change between weekdays and weekends is more dramatic in 2020 than 2024 which seems to speak to the limited activity choices in that year. 

***Step 4: Data Visualization 2:***
```{r plot2}
# Filter and prepare the 2024 data
duration_2024_df <- citibike_combined_df %>%
  filter(year == 2024) %>%
  drop_na(month, member_casual, rideable_type, duration) 

# Check the prepared subset
print(duration_2024_df)

# Create the multi-panel distribution plot
duration_2024_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) + 
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 2) +               
  labs(
    title = "Impact of Month, Membership Status, and Bike Type on Ride Duration (2024)",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (Minutes)", #Duration assumed to be in minutes according to google search
    fill = "Membership Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold")
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50)) 
```
***Plot 2 Comments:***
We see that while rides from members stay relatively stable across the months and bikes (with slight increase on electric bike in July), causal rides change by bike type and months. For casual rides, there is a increase in ride duration from January to July and from electric bike to classic bike. The change in weather across the months has been discussed previously, but here we also see a change between classic and electric bike probably due to price differences. 

For non-members, there is a unlock fee for classic bikes and then you get the first 30 minutes free but for an electric bike you have to pay for every minute. That's why it's more worth-it to ride your full 30 min. for the classic bike and stay on the electric bike for as short a time as possible for casual riders. This explains the decrease in duration from classic boke to electric bike for casual riders across both months. 

Finally between members, casual rides are generally longer than member rides across bike types and months. This is probably due to pricing as well with members getting a better deal from increased usage while casual riders limit usage (to avoid paying unlock fees) but try to get most of their 30 minutes for casual bikes and only travelling longer distances with the electric bike (otherwise walking or classic bike are probably better and cheaper options).
